title: 🏘️ Eryndor Living Atlas VI — Patchwork Villages & Folktale Crossroads
rawNotionMarkup: Creator-directed addition to the Eryndor Living Atlas, Year 3,847: patchwork villages and folkloric crossroads. The creator wants some towns with the lively, improbable mix of people found in ensemble fairy tales: Pigfolk and Wolvenkin, little Brownies, Goblins, Gnomes, Pixies, Satyrs, Trolls, Foxfolk, Harpies and others as neighbors, shopkeepers, rivals and families. This is an atmosphere and social-design direction, not a request to insert characters, storylines or copyrighted locations from another fictional work. The settlements below are new, adjustable worldbuilding, not places Gloin has already visited. All residents belong to previously established intelligent peoples; no new sentient species is declared by implication. ## Sixfold world census is now the current baseline — 21 November 2026 Population resimulation completed: The creator explicitly accepted a 6× revision of previously simulated Year 3847 populations. The current modeled world total is 2,062.800 million residents (formerly 343.800m), with Avarra 1,019.760m, Tharvorn 171.000m, Sahrad 282.222m, Orundel 393.600m and Vaelora 196.218m. The 28-people by five-continent matrix, 133 previously quantified named settlement/Throne entries, the 18 resident categories of Bramblebridge, and the 8 other quantified patchwork places, plus habitat and carrying-capacity constraints, are audited in Eryndor Living Census XII — Sixfold Population & Carrying-Capacity Audit. Priority and supersession: All old 343.8m, 24m Khazari, 22m Seven Thrones, 18m Eldar, 31m Urakai and 3.8m Karak-Varn figures in the preserved legacy text are superseded as current demographic estimates by 6× figures. They remain intact only as historical reference or original simulation baselines. New: 144m global Khazari; 132m Seven-Throne domain subtotal included in the 144m; 22.8m Karak-Varn included in the Thrones. Do NOT add these overlapping totals. Long-lived peoples retain unchanged birth rates, and any specific community may still face housing, food, water and supply crises because the new populations are not equally concentrated. This is a historical-scale editorial resimulation, not 6× births during the current play session. No old ancient First Throne uncertain peak estimate or unnamed uncensused species is automatically multiplied. Gloin's Year 3847, Era of Crowns, Fifth Age campaign remains paused at Hadrik's desk, Autumn Day 22 \~11:25 AM. ## Worldwide fairy-tale peoples — full communities and classic folklore lifestyles coexist (creator rule, 21 November 2026) Creator's explicit generalization of the Ogre rule: Throughout all of Eryndor, across all five continents and islands, the established fairy-tale and whimsical peoples should occur both in their recognizable folkloric settings AND in completely developed villages, town districts, island settlements, societies and mixed urban communities. A few individuals or a single token village are not sufficient. There can be whole settlements populated predominantly by the same people, as well as mixed-species market towns and independent families. These are normal lived places, with children, elders, occupations, neighbors, law, trade, festivities, histories, economies and disagreements. The specific Ogre precedent is real: some live in lone swamp huts, others form sizable Ogre swamp villages, island communities or marshland clans, and still others live in cities or unrelated climates. Never impose that archetypal lifestyle on every member of a people. Broader application as illustrative environmental/cultural possibilities (not rigid habitat assignments): Some Goblins may maintain burrow hamlets, crowded trading quarters, road camps or market towns; some Pixies may occupy full treetop or garden settlements rather than solitary flowers; some Brownies/Boggarts may maintain farm-edge hamlets, old manor quarters or hedgerow communities; some Trolls may inhabit bridge-side family settlements, marsh villages or highland communities; some Satyrs/Fauns may form orchard/woodland communities; some Gnomes may have villages, learned workshops or river towns; some Mushroom folk may inhabit damp forest floor or cavern settlements; some Harpies may have cliffside towns or roost communities; some Minotaurs may build broad-street towns or agricultural centers. Apply the same principle to other established folklore-like peoples (Kobolds, Halflings, Giants, Centaurs, animal-featured peoples, Merfolk, etc.) where their actual biology, terrain and societies allow. Not every example must appear in every region. The creator may later change or reject particular examples without invalidating the general rule. Tone and social variation: Preserve the classic fairy-tale charm, danger, strangeness, myth and occasional dark menace. Some hermits and enclaves really are frightening, hostile, predatory, magical or unusual; others are welcoming or ordinary, and settlements have internal differences. No sapient people is uniformly sweet, stupid, murderous, comical, primitive, isolated or predetermined morally good/evil by ancestry. Modern cultural and political realities, including western fear of Ogres and distrust/discrimination against Goblins rooted in eastern–western wars, continue to exist alongside these real communities. Civilizations can include both long-established regional homelands and diaspora/mixed towns. Map and simulation guardrails: New atlas maps should show clusters and networks of villages, island towns, marsh communities, woodland boroughs and distinctive local settlements across the vast expanse rather than isolated one-off folklore pins. Their places must have food, water, exchange, transport, protection and geography appropriate to scale. Do not invent exact population counts, rulers, species-specific fertility, additional moons, universal magical powers or a new kingdom merely from an illustration. The current sixfold population model is redistributed rather than inflated. Avarra's seven Throne mountain ring/Veiled Inland Sea, the vast Letharion forest, two different western human culture belts, eastern Urakai badlands and very rare/unsettled Eastern Grasslands Urakai remain as most recently corrected. This creator-level worldbuilding doesn't advance Gloin's campaign. ## What a patchwork settlement IS and IS NOT - A patchwork settlement is a community where genuinely different species, sizes, traditions and reputations live side by side in a shared civic life. One street may hold a Pigfolk baker's home, a Kobold pottery kiln, a Brownie family inside a purpose-built miniature courtyard, a Wolvenkin carpenter's workshop, a Pixie-owned seed shop and an Ogre's freight yard. - Humor matters: petty feuds over fences, ridiculous town ordinances, tiny stools beside enormous tavern benches, unusual family dinners, rival guilds, stubborn festivals, mistaken assumptions and good-natured oddballs. Not every interaction is a world-ending emergency. - This mixture exists for grounded reasons: border trade, unusual asylum charters, old shared disasters, market privileges, transported craft skills, religious toleration, adopted families, intermarriage where possible and mixed mercenary retirement towns. It must not become a universal species-city template. - Their inhabitants have real politics, employment, poverty, crime, housing, friendship, medicine, taxes and personal flaws. A feared Troll or Wolvenkin can be a beloved neighbor; a supposedly harmless Pixie can be an unscrupulous lender. Nobody's morality is predetermined by biological ancestry. - Scale matters: tiny residents need safe footpaths, small goods, sheltered bedrooms, specialty tools and protection from carts and predators; large residents need broad doorways, massive meals, reinforced floors and higher transport costs. Flying people need wind and landing space. Merfolk cannot casually inhabit an ordinary dry tavern without water infrastructure. Human-size streets alone cannot plausibly house every species. - Romance/relations: friendships, marriages, adoptive kinship and households exist across cultures. Do not assume biological hybrid offspring are possible between unrelated species without explicit biological and magical establishment. - Danger still exists: outside the walls, a predatory band, angry herd, harsh winter or dishonest reeve can be serious. Patchwork towns can be delightful and occasionally unsettling, without becoming cartoon physics or universal pacifism. Inside the walls, even a well-liked resident can commit genuinely lethal violence. A physical confrontation with a large Ogre, Troll, Minotaur, Giant or other powerful individual could overwhelm an ordinary village watch. Danger is determined by the individual, circumstances and actual capabilities, not by assuming every such person is a latent monster. - Towns may be known locally but unknown to Gloin. Some mixed hamlets truly hide from official maps. The reader/worldbuilder may know their coordinates while Gloin must find directions by conversation, travel and chance. ## Creator's darker-tone rule — charm never guarantees safety Binding world-design correction: The creator explicitly said that a seemingly friendly Ogre in a mixed-species town could suddenly become violent and go on a deadly rampage; townsfolk and guards would have to stop the attacker, potentially using lethal force if the threat cannot otherwise be ended. This is a possible emergent event, not a predetermined incident involving Gadra Mossback or an assertion that Ogres inevitably become violent. A serious fantasy world contains charming towns and crime, murder, catastrophic mistakes, abuse of power, war, anger, trauma, madness, intoxication, greed, vengeance, dangerous accidents and conflicts that cannot all be solved with words. No supernatural mechanism is necessary without evidence. - Individual agency and unpredictability: A once-friendly resident may become dangerous; conversely, a frightening resident may remain steadfastly peaceful. The decisive cause can be known, disputed, hidden or ordinary. Never make a particular species' violent nature biologically inevitable or reduce violence to a simplistic racial stereotype. - Proportional response and consequences: Town watch may sound bells, evacuate children and tiny residents, form shield lines, try to stop the attacker, call competent defenders, capture if realistically possible, or kill in immediate defense of life. Guards can be injured, outmatched or arrive too late; they are not invincible. Defenders can err or act bravely, and legal scrutiny follows. - Serious stakes: Deaths, burns, wrecked homes, orphaned children, grieving relatives, injured guards, displacement, rebuilding costs, court hearings and changes in local relationships persist. A fatal rampage must not be immediately played for slapstick laughter; later everyday humor may return naturally. - No outcome fixed in advance: It is not canon that Gadra or any named resident will rampage, that Gloin will witness the event, that the watch will win, or that lethal action will always be warranted. Such events arise only during actual in-world time and play, for grounded reasons or credible uncertainty. A player may intervene, flee, help the wounded, refuse involvement or never hear of it. - No guaranteed fairytale shield: The charming architecture, cozy inns and funny disputes do not give any adult character, child, guard, or adventurer invulnerability. Conversely, not every market visit should devolve into an indiscriminate slaughter; day-to-day life remains plausible and varied. - Aftermath is part of the story: Authorities distinguish self-defense from revenge and murder. Residents may blame the wrong person or species; responsible institutions should investigate actual individuals and evidence instead of punishing an entire people. Intense violence has economic, political and psychological consequences in the world. Example of what the creator means, not an already-happened event: A powerful Ogre who was welcomed in town for years loses control during a confrontation, breaks through a market stall and severely injures bystanders. The watch tries to contain the threat but some guards are overmatched; a veteran guard, another resident or a visiting fighter might end the danger through physical force. Some may die. The village is shaken; the incident is investigated and households must live with its consequences. The exact cause, participants, intervention and final outcome are not written into canon. ## Bramblebridge — the strongest example, near Gloin's potential western route New location: Western Avarra foothills, on the westbound wagon road between Copperspan and Staghollow, approximately 190 km by road west of Karak-Varn. It sits where an arched stone road bridge crosses a productive brook with apple orchards, mills, reeds and woodlots. Its existence does not overwrite Copperspan (\~90 km), Staghollow (\~275 km) or Nine Oaks (\~340 km). Scale: Large village / small market town of approximately 3,600 permanent residents. It developed around a century-old Free Hearth Charter, a local agreement allowing different-sized peoples to settle, trade and testify in court as individuals. The charter and age are newly designed history, not recovered from a previous conversation. The town's council can repeal or amend regulations through its established procedures; nobody is exempt from prosecution just because the town is whimsical. ### Population mix (resident bookkeeping exactly totals 3,600) | People | Residents | Typical local roles, not biological restrictions | | --- | --- | --- | | Halflings | 620 | Farming, inns, food merchants, household gardens | | Pigfolk | 470 | Milling, builders, cooks, boat owners, farmers | | Goblins | 450 | Merchants, leather goods, carpenters, warehouse clerks | | Humans | 340 | Bakers, farm tenants, drivers, watch, scribes | | Foxfolk | 330 | Couriers, traders, orchard guardians, bookkeepers | | Gnomes | 310 | Mechanics, bridge repair, maps, makers of tiny tools | | Wolvenkin | 270 | Forestry, carpentry, guards, farming, music | | Kobolds | 260 | Brickworks, drainage pipes, storage galleries | | Brownies/Boggarts | 180 | Independent small-scale crafts, gardens and property owners | | Satyrs/Fauns | 140 | Orchards, herding, musicians, sawmill families | | Eldar | 70 | Herbalists, woodlands liaison, legal clerks | | Khazari | 70 | Quarry stone, bridge inspection, wheelwright trade | | Pixies | 45 | Seeds, textiles, canopy messenger craft | | Cowfolk | 25 | Dairy, carts, smallholdings | | Ogres | 6 | Heavy lifting, road and cart maintenance, personal lives | | Trolls | 5 | Bridge maintenance, fisheries and ordinary households | | Harpies | 4 | Watch service and courier work, weather permitting | | Minotaurs | 5 | Carting, stone foundations, independent trade | | Total | 3,600 | No racial neighborhood exclusively required | Village layout: Broadwheel Street runs between a westgate caravan yard and a bridge. Little-Lane has small stairless homes and tiny sheltered courts for Brownies and short residents. Bellroof Terrace rises to a Pixie-accessible series of balconies and wind-sheltered ropeways. The Lower Brook hosts a watermill and fishery; Cinder Yard has a Kobold kiln and blacksmithy with strict fire control. Tall Door Square has an Ogre-sized freight store and reinforced meeting hall. Tangle Orchard supplies fruit and pays a grove-right fee to a nearby woodland council. The bridge crosses a natural stream; no ancient mystical resonance is presumed. Economy: Apple and pear harvest, barley and vegetables, watermill flour, bread and preserved fruit, pottery, axles, wagon repairs, wool, dairy, woodland herbs, a seasonal cattle market and occasional escorted freight. Surrounding hamlets supply extra food and fuel; 3,600 people cannot survive on one enchanted apple tree. The weekly market brings short-term visitors who do not appear in the resident census. An autumn apple fair can double street traffic for a day but is not a permanent population jump. Civic law: A seven-member rotating Hearth Council with elected representatives from property holders, household co-ops and trade wards, with at-large seats not allocated by biology. A Magistrate hears contract disputes. The watch of around 26 full/part-time people and militia call-ups cannot defeat a professional army; traders hire escorts. The oddest real ordinance requires cart drivers to ring a bell before crossing Little-Lane because small neighbors are difficult to see. It is a safety rule, not a silly magical law. ### Residents Gloin could meet (not automatically known to him) - Mayor Tilda Brackenwheel, a Pigfolk miller and three-term council chair. Warmly formidable, deeply invested in river levees, suspicious of anyone claiming a free lunch. - Bren Hushfur, a towering, silver-muzzled Wolvenkin baker who bakes exemplary seed loaves. Children tell exaggerated stories about his teeth; he is weary of those stories, but he can become genuinely frightening if threatened. A former militia veteran, not a secretly scripted monster. - Nib Ketterspark, a Goblin merchant, sharp dresser and shameless haggler. Maintains the market's actual weighing scales and reports forged weights when profitable or principled. - Pippry Fen, a Brownie shoemaker whose workshop has a perfectly legal miniature front door hidden inside the bigger shopfront; vehemently opposes being called a household spirit. - Orrin Bell-Nose, a Gnome bridge mechanic who will explain the whole waterwheel in excruciating detail unless someone changes the subject. - Thessa Reedstep, a Satyr orchard keeper and town festival marshal. She maintains complicated grazing agreements with six nearby farms and will absolutely argue about them. - Yarra Siltroot, a Kobold drainage engineer with a terrible sense of humor and rigorous fire-safety records. - Mara Quicktwig, a Pixie seed-seller who operates from an upper-level box-stall and organizes public petitions about wind-sheltered walkways. - Old Sorn, a retired Troll bridge-setter and fisherman who never accepts payment to guard a bridge he no longer owns, and hates the word “troll toll.” - Gadra Mossback, an Ogre freight porter who enjoys delicate needlework after long shifts and takes public safety extremely seriously. Character-web complications: Mayor Tilda's brother owns half the flour mills and stands to benefit from a new bridge toll. Bren's bakery and Nib's market stall dispute a delivery alley. Orrin thinks the stone bridge needs urgent reinforcement; Sorn says the foundation is sound but drainage is failing. The little residents want an additional protected crossing; big-wagon merchants object to the cost. People can disagree fiercely and still sit together at dinner. ### Everyday scene: midday at the Crooked Teapot At the inn, two Halfling drovers are debating a very inaccurate map. A Pigfolk mason is arguing that the new chimney must be brick, while a Wolvenkin carpenter says the roof will not bear the weight. A Goblin clerk is trying to tax a basket of mushrooms that was a gift, a Pixie is loudly demanding a refund for a miniature umbrella, and an Ogre carefully holds a teacup on two fingers as the innkeeper repairs an extra-wide doorframe. Nobody is cast as a “big bad” by species. On a back bench, a suspicious traveler might genuinely be listening for bounty notices. The town is a lived place, not a skit performed on Gloin's arrival. Optional local problems: Bridge maintenance debt; an innocent Wolvenkin falsely blamed for livestock losses; apple trees with an ordinary fungus threatening farm income; a caravan company trying to raise market rents; a vanished flour shipment with evidence of petty theft rather than ancient magic. Each can evolve or resolve without Gloin. An outsider is not appointed savior. ## Other patchwork towns scattered around the five continents | Settlement | Continent / location | Model population | Species blend and distinct atmosphere | Real livelihood and friction | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Wickerwold | Avarra, hidden alderwood near the Staghollow orchards | 230 | Brownies, Pixies, Halflings, Satyrs, two Trolls and a few Gnomes. Tiny lanes, patchwork gardens and old arboreal bridges; outsiders often walk past its unmarked footpath. | Beekeeping, herbs, wickerwork; a local fire-break dispute puts miniature homes at risk | | Nine-Tin Bells | Avarra, Shattered Coast inland inlet near merchant routes | 7,800 | Pigfolk, Foxfolk, Goblins, Harpies, Gnomes, humans and frequent Merfolk visitors at a purpose-built tidal landing. A bustling, oddly dressed, noisy port-market town. | Rope, oysters, ship repairs, weather flags, port charges; seabed access belongs to a separate Merfolk polity | | Candleburrow | Tharvorn, sheltered southern forest valley | 1,450 | Trolls, Ogres, Bearfolk, Wolvenkin, Brownies, Gnomes, Goblins and humans. Low warm doors connect to a high-ceiling meeting house and snow roofed lanes. | Firewood, berries, salt fish, winter craft, heated granaries; winter firewood allocation arguments | | Saffronstep | Sahrad, secondary canal on northern irrigated river valley | 1,950 | Halflings, Kobolds, Lionfolk, Elephantfolk, Pigfolk, Brownies, Gnomes and humans. Mosaic courtyard homes, shaded arcade stalls and miniature cisterns. | Irrigation, date cakes, spices, pottery; canal ration rights govern who can grow what | | Tanglelock | Orundel, central river-federation trade crossroads | 5,500 | Goblins, Foxfolk, Tigerfolk, Pigfolk, Kobolds, Gnomes, Minotaurs, Centaurs, humans and seasonal Harpies. Bridges of different widths and endless gossip. | Barges, lock repairs, smoked fish, market arbitration; crowded crossing and ferry-toll politics | | Thornhollow | Vaelora, Elderwood and great-lakes frontier | 2,100 | Satyrs, Pixies, Foxfolk, Pigfolk, Brownies, Goblins, Eldar and a few friendly but formidable Troll and Ogre households. Fungus lantern gardens, canopy stalls and deep porch houses. | Forest mushrooms, fruit, boat timber, cider; logging licenses conflict with Ent grove agreements | | Shellbutton Reach | Vaelora, tidal harbor beside the western sea | 960 surface + separate underwater visitors | Pigfolk, Gnomes, Harpies, Kobolds, Foxfolk and sailors, with Merfolk trade barges meeting at saltwater basins. | Fish drying, salvage, harbor lanterns; a pier-sharing dispute and strong tides | | Whistleberry Camp | Avarra, transient autumn orchard gathering between Copperspan and Nine Oaks | \~350 autumn residents, fewer in winter | Halfling, Foxfolk, Goblin and Satyr travelling craftspeople, plus a handful of Brownie families. Many painted carts, tents, cookfires and storytelling circles. | Fruit harvest, fairs, mobile repairs, travelling theaters; grazing-right tensions and seasonal movement | Do not confuse a harvest gathering with a permanent village population. Crossroads and hidden hamlets may mix people differently. A Pigfolk family in Sahrad can be unrelated to the family in Bramblebridge; species identity is not one world-spanning ethnicity or political alliance. ## Magical concealment of fairy-tale settlements — worldwide creator rule (21 November 2026) Creator-established extension of the living fairy-tale world: A large number of communities, settlements, hamlets, islands, groves, cave networks and even sizable villages or towns of Eryndor's many established intelligent peoples may be hidden through magic. Concealment may work in concert with ordinary remoteness, woodland cover, wetlands, confusing terrain or political secrecy. This is a real and widespread option throughout the five continents and islands, not a single token magical village or a privilege reserved for one species. An Ogre swamp village or island, Pixie canopy settlement, Aelwyn court, Gnome or Goblin hill community, Mushroom-folk cavern network and other fairy-tale settlements may be partly or wholly unknown even to nearby outsiders. Entire populated enclaves can exist among otherwise surveyed landscapes. Not an automatic species trait: Many Ogres, Goblins, Pixies, Fae, Gnomes and other folk also live openly in public villages, mixed markets, ports, cities and rural districts. Do not make every settlement magical, invisible, isolated, safe or inaccessible. Magical concealment need not be permanent, perfect, universal or the same everywhere. Some people can know a hidden settlement and trade with it; inhabitants can leave and visit outsiders; concealment can be incomplete, fallible, selective, locally maintained, or occasionally overcome, but no exact mechanism, bypass, moon assignment or failure rule is canonized merely by this principle. Even when hidden, settlements require viable food/water, internal social relations, waste disposal, crafts and trade according to local ecology. Magic consistency and geographic mystery: The moons are real sources of lunar magic; people know that but not which moon governs which effect or how lunar magic works. The planet independently generates Natural Magic, and individual peoples maintain their already established traditions (Khazari Runecraft/Deepcraft, Eldar, Aelwyn Fae, Pixie/fairy, Gnome, etc.). Concealment may be produced by suitable magic but is not automatically a new universal discipline or explained by one known moon, divine force or prayer. The Veiled Inland Sea is already an unusual hidden region: its established external inaccessibility and interior shore community network remain, but its precise concealment mechanism is separately unresolved and must not be copied onto all hidden villages. Atlas and campaign safeguards: Regional maps can depict known hidden communities on private informed charts with appropriate uncertainty, while public maps may omit them or record conflicting rumors. Do not populate all blank areas with named settlements or announce secrets to characters without discovery. Preserve the creator's 6× modeled world population without double counting residents of hidden communities and leave uncensused enclaves truly uncertain. Gloin's campaign remains paused at Autumn Day 22, Year 3847 of the Era of Crowns, Fifth Age, approximately 11:25 AM; the character has no new automatic knowledge of any secret location. ## Hidden / uncharted counterparts — leave real discovery space For every named patchwork settlement above, there can be additional unnamed hamlets, abandoned villages and seasonal meeting places. Do not pre-fill every forest and gorge with names before the narrative needs them. The GM can preconstruct an unseen community's government, population, water, food, trades and conflicts, then reveal it only through in-world travel or information. - A hidden Gnome, Brownie, Goblin and Pixie settlement inside the roots of enormous Vaeloran trees may have no permanent marked road. - A riverside community of Cowfolk, Pigfolk, Foxfolk and Kobold farming families can share a market hall under a human lord, with their own household agreements. - A ruined customs post occupied by lawful mixed traders may resemble an outlaw camp to an unfamiliar observer. - A northern hamlet of Troll, Ogre, Bearfolk and human families can be terrifying to strangers and perfectly normal to its resident children. Biological rule: Existing sentient species include Pigfolk, Wolvenkin, Foxfolk, Brownies/Boggarts, Gnomes, Goblins, Pixies, Satyrs, etc. Do not create Mousefolk or copy famous literary fairytale personalities merely because the creator gave a loose comparison involving “little pigs, three blind mice and a big bad wolf.” Those examples communicate whimsical ensemble vibe, not direct insertion of specific characters or authorization of a new species. New sapient peoples can be added explicitly later if the creator wishes. ## Player introduction and canon boundaries - World-known vs character-known: Bramblebridge and Nine-Tin Bells have regional market reputations; Wickerwold could be genuinely absent from public maps. Gloin has not automatically heard of them and has not entered their inns. - Geographical link: Bramblebridge's \~190 km position is compatible with the established road sequence Karak-Varn → Copperspan (\~90) → Staghollow (\~275) → Nine Oaks (\~340). Detailed turn-offs require an in-world map or guide. - No premature adventure: The campaign remains paused at Autumn Day 22, Year 3,847, \~11:25 AM at Hadrik's archive desk with Maela, before Gloin answers. Nothing on these pages causes NPCs or the calendar to move by itself. - Non-exhaustiveness: The 9 named patchwork places are representative and scattered; Eryndor still contains innumerable other hamlets, farmsteads, caravan camps and towns with different mixed or single-peoples identities. They must be physically, economically and socially credible; some are eccentric, some serious, some grim, some cozy. - Creator control: All new names, numbers and local details are subject to change. Do not silently retcon established original chat, and do not require Gloin to ever visit a patchwork town.
